note: A place-by-place sweep of FamilySearch's indexed Croatian and Istrian records for this surname and its variants, run in September 2026 across sixty towns and parishes from Muggia to Senj. What follows is where the name is indexed, where it is not, and — importantly — why a blank is not an absence.
lead: The archive had searched by name. This searches by place, one parish at a time, which is the only way to see the shape of a surname across a province. Sixty places; twenty-one return the name; thirty-nine return nothing. Two of the twenty-one push the surname back further in Istria than anything else this project has found. **Read the counts as weight, not population** — and read the blanks with the section at the foot of this page, which shows that the search's place parameter does not filter at all.
method: For each place, the top hundred indexed persons matching Defranceschi were pulled and kept only if the record's own place text actually names that town and the name is a Franceschi form. Counts are of matched index entries, not of distinct people — a single baptism can appear more than once — so read them as weight, not as population.

clusters.who: Antonio, Mattio, Pietro, Maria, Virginia Lambertina Defranceschi
clusters.note: The heaviest concentration anywhere in the sweep, and it starts in 1742 — two years after the Giovanni Battista whom Kobler traced arriving from the County of Pazin «intorno al 1740». Carlo's own account of the Fiume branch lands exactly here.

clusters.who: Natale Mattio, Angelo, Vitorio, Elisabetta, Irene De Franceschi
clusters.note: Carlo's book names Franceschi among the noble families of Pola «venuti da Capodistria» before the plague of 1631, and a Sabba de Franceschi of Bologna licensed in 1562 to settle families there. This is a third and much larger presence, a century and a half later.
With Premantura and Medulin this makes a real southern-Istrian group around the tip of the peninsula, entirely separate from the central-Istrian line.
All the Senj hits are Franceschini or Franceskini, not Defranceschi — a different formation of the same root, and a caution against treating the two as one family.

clusters.who: Mattio, Domenico Gasparo, Zuana, Marina, Maria Maddalena De Franceschi
clusters.note: The oldest cluster in Istria, and the most interesting single result of the sweep. A settled De Franceschi household at Svetvinčenat in the 1670s, bearing the name Zuana — the Venetian form of Giovanni, the same form as the Zuane of the 1679 Mione list. It is contemporaneous with everything the Carnia argument turns on, and nobody in this project had looked at Svetvinčenat.

clusters.who: Carlo Franceschi, Amelia and Mario Franceschini, Iolanda Franceschi
Giorgius, Nicolò, Giorgio, Margarita Maria, Nadalina Defranceschi
clusters.note: Promontore, at the very southern tip.

clusters.who: Joannem, Maria Anna, Antoniam, Nodburgam Defranceschi, Francisca Paula Franceskini
clusters.note: Including a Nodburga — a rare Germanic saint's name, and one the family already holds a record image of.

clusters.who: Franciscus, Joannes Aloysius, Josephus, Maria Defranceschi

clusters.note: Carlo was appointed to the court at Rovinj in 1850 and his son Camillo took refuge there in the war.

The single earliest indexed occurrence of the surname anywhere in Istria: 1615, at Albona. Sixty-four years before the Mione headmen's list, and eighty-five before the date Carlo gives for his family's arrival.

clusters.who: Conraddus Vincentius and Liberatus Francus Xaverius Defranceschi
clusters.note: Two elaborate Latin names in one year. Vincenzo is one of the names Carlo says the Zadar branch keeps, and a Vincenzo was Chancellor of the County of Pazin in that century.
A compound Slavicised form. The map the family keeps traces Barban emigrants to Moselle, Cannes and Charleville in France.

clusters.who: Anna Maria Defranceschi, José de Franceschi

clusters.note: One entry, and it carries the exact name-form of Carlo's great-great-grandfather.

caveat.heading: Why the blanks prove nothing at all
caveat.text: Gračišće returns nothing. Gologorica returns nothing. Crikvenica returns nothing. This archive has, in its own files, the 1863 baptism at Gračišće, the Status Animarum of Gallignana, the 1890 baptism at Klenovica and four Crikvenica register entries — all of them for this family, none of them findable by this search. The reason is simple: those registers are on FamilySearch as browse-only images that no volunteer has indexed. A blank in the table above means «not typed up», not «not there». It is the single most important thing to understand about searching this surname, and it is why the real work of this project has been done in scans and archives rather than in search boxes.
caveat.then: Read the other way, the blanks are a work list. Every parish above with a nil return and a known register is a place where a morning of page-turning could produce something no search will ever surface.

reading.h: There is no single Istrian family of this name
reading.t: The sweep shows at least four groups that do not obviously touch: a Rijeka–Bakar concentration from 1742; a Pula–Ližnjan–Premantura–Medulin group in the far south from about 1778; a scatter across the north-west at Kaštelir, Oprtalj, Roč, Šterna and Vrsar; and the central-Istrian line at Gračišće and Gologorica that this archive follows, which the index cannot see at all. Add Labin in 1615 and Svetvinčenat in the 1670s and the picture is of a patronymic surname arising and arriving repeatedly, not of one trunk.

reading.h: But two results are worth chasing hard
reading.t: Svetvinčenat 1674–1710 and Labin 1615 are both older than the Mione list of 1679, and both older than the 1700 date Carlo gives for his family reaching Istria. If the De Franceschi were already at Albona in 1615, the tidy story of a single Carnian arrival around 1700 is at best incomplete.

Šterna, 1807, «Gio Batta De Franceschi». Carlo's great-great-grandfather was Giambattista del fu Leonardo, who built the Gologorica house in 1711. This is a different man in a different century, but the name-form runs in a family and Šterna is two hours' walk from Oprtalj, where the Franceschini are.

next: Svetvinčenat parish registers, 1650–1720 — the oldest cluster and the least examined. Ask whether the Mattio and Zuana of the 1670s have parents in the book.
Labin (Albona) 1600–1650, for the Aloysius Defranceschi of 1615.
Rijeka 1740–1760, for the Giovanni Battista who came from the County of Pazin — Carlo's own great-uncle's line.
Ližnjan, Premantura and Medulin as one southern group: are they one family across three parishes?
And the thirty-nine blanks, one register at a time.

resweep.heading: The whole thing again, properly — 18,840 records, eighteen towns
resweep.lead: David asked a question that took the ground out from under this page: if the method was wrong for Bakar, was it wrong everywhere? It was. The earlier sweeps matched place-names against a short extracted string instead of the whole record, and they stopped after a couple of hundred results a spelling. So the whole thing was rebuilt as a resumable machine — six spellings of the surname across five country filters, thirty jobs, each paged to the index's own ceiling, every record matched whole — and re-run from nothing. It read 18,840 records and found 664 distinct people with a place. Here is the corrected distribution, and it is not the one this page used to show.
table: Kobler's Fiume stock and everything after it. The oldest cluster in the sweep and still the largest.
Second, and this archive had barely looked. A continuous parish record across two hundred and thirty-six years.
Third. The village where «Defrančeski Ante» gave two lire to a Croatian paper in 1920.
Where Brhan's Zuane Prencis was brother-in-law to a Sebastiano de Franceschi.
Mostly Omiš. The earliest date anywhere in the sweep.
Carlo's town in his later years.
A single household, in four years, with Habsburg baptismal names.
Five of them spelt with the háček.
Both incomers from Italy — Borgoricco and Genoa. Not this family.
Battista De Franceschi, born 1879 at Ovaro — the parish the 1679 list was drawn up in.

rows.lab: Svetvinčenat begins in 1628 — corrected 13 September 2026
rows.text: **Corrected.** This row said the parish begins in 1666. It begins in **1628**. «Alì 21 Decembre — **Elena fiola di Francescho di Franceschi et di Eufemia sua consorte**» — Svetvinčenat, Births 1589–1646, image 58, read at full magnification. Thirty-eight years earlier than anything below, and **thirty-three years before Moncalvo di Pisino**, which this archive had treated as the family's first Istrian appearance. It was missed by two sweeps because its place field says only «Croazia, Austria». The whole finding, and the method that found it, are on the reading page. What follows is still true of the 1663–1708 book and is left as written. Colotta De Franceschi, born 10 October and baptised 24 October 1666. Fioretta, born 18 November, baptised 22 November 1666. Franceschina, 1667. Mattia, 1669. Anto and Giacomo, 1671. «Piero De Francesich», February 1672 — the surname already being pulled into a Slavic shape. Giovanna, 1673. Mattio, 1674. Zuana, 1688. Batista and Flora, 1692. Two children of this name were carried to the font at Svetvinčenat in a single autumn, five years after the family's first recorded appearance at Moncalvo at the other end of Istria. The 1734 household book was not the beginning; it was already the third generation.

rows.lab: And the register names the very people Brhan found in the notarial papers
rows.text: Brhan, working the protocols of the Sanvincenti notaries, named «D.no Vittorio De Franceschi» among the Carnian landholders, a «Gasparo De Franceschi, carnico pure lui», and the kinswomen Pasqua and Antonia named in Maria Zanco's will. All four surface in the register sweep independently: Vitorio Defranceschi, born 1758, buried 8 November 1812; Victorius, born 1845, died 25 May 1897; Gasparo, Gaspari, Gaspero and Gaspo De Franceschi across the eighteenth century; Pasqua, and Pasqua Vitoria, born 16 December 1773; Antonia. Two entirely different classes of record, produced by different clerks for different purposes, naming the same household.

rows.lab: A household at Pazin in the 1790s, and it is not one this archive knows
rows.text: Eight records in four years, and the names are Habsburg-official names, not Istrian peasant ones: Anastasius Defrancoschi, born 1789, dead 5 March 1793; Liberatus Franciscus Xaverius, born 1791, dead 14 February 1792; Conraddus Vincentius, baptised 22 February 1793; Liberatus Maria Xaverius; Maria Leopoldina; Vincentius Defranceski. Two infants buried in thirteen months. This is a family that arrived, buried two children in the county town and moved on — and it stands at exactly the place and period of the unidentified «Count Damian de Franceschis» this archive has been carrying as an open question.

rows.lab: Five Zagreb graves with the háček
rows.text: Marija Defrančeski, 1884–1971. Milan Defrančeski, 10 February 1923 – 24 May 2001. Milka Defrančeski Kirin, 1918–1990. Dragutin Defranceski, 1925–2004. And Zdenkica Defrančeski, 1943–1945 — a child of two, buried in Zagreb in the last year of the war. The Croatian spelling of this surname is not a scribal accident and it is not only in the newspapers: there are people under stones with it.

rows.lab: The oldest date in the whole sweep is in Dalmatia
rows.text: Gioannes Maria De Franceschi, born 1581, died 20 March 1645, buried at Omiš. Then Mandalina, baptised 14 November 1634; Nicolaa, 12 January 1644; Francesco, 1 August 1657; and Nicolo, born 1626, buried at Split on 18 May 1716 at ninety. A Dalmatian line of the name running from the year the Venetians finished the walls of Omiš to the eighteenth century, and no connection to Istria has been shown.

rows.lab: And Fiume is older than anything in Istria
rows.text: Francischina, 7 November 1620. Catterina, 15 November 1621. Franciscu, 23 February 1625. Joannem Antonio, 6 September 1626. Gioanna Victoria, 19 April 1628. Maria, 9 September 1632. Zuane, 13 April 1632. The clerk writes «de Francesco» in the 1620s and «de Franceschi» by the later 1620s — the surname settling into its form inside one register.

rows.lab: What the sweep does not settle
rows.text: Bakar does not appear here, because the town groups were built before the Bakar correction and Bakar was not one of them; the separate Bakar query stands at twelve people over three generations and is published on its own page. Gologorica returns one record and Gračišće none — not because the family was not there, which the parish books prove it was, but because those registers are not in this index. An index sweep measures what has been indexed. It is a map of the record, not of the people.

resweep.method2: Six spellings — De Franceschi, Defranceschi, Defranceski, De Franceski, Defrančeski, Franceschi — each run against five country filters, thirty jobs in all, each paged to the index's own ceiling of about 1,400. Every record was matched whole, as JSON, against thirty-six place patterns, rather than against a short extracted summary string. That is the fix. The earlier method matched a truncated field and therefore missed most of what was there.

filter.heading: The place parameter does not filter. Tested, and it does not.
filter.lead: On 9 September 2026 this archive tested the search endpoint its own sweep is built on. The result changes how every place-based number here should be read.

rows.lab: The test
rows.text:
The same query was run against FamilySearch's persona search with the place parameter set to **Vižinada**, **Draguč**, **Dubrovnik**, **Vodnjan**, **Rovinj**, **Gračišće**, **Kaštelir**, **Ližnjan**, and to **«Zzzznowhere»** and **«Atlantis»**.

**Every single one returned the same total: 3,652.**

`q.anyPlace` is a **relevance boost, not a filter**. It changes the order of the results and nothing else. A place it does not recognise is silently ignored and you get the whole set back, with no error and no warning.

rows.lab: And two real villages come back identical
rows.text:
**Vižinada** and **Draguč** return the *same records, in the same order*. They cannot be told apart by this route at all. **Dubrovnik** returns exactly what no place parameter returns — the unfiltered head of the list.

`f.recordPlace` *is* a genuine filter, but it rejects plain town names: `Vodnjan`, `Rovinj` and a numeric place id all return **0**, and a name with spaces is refused outright — «Filter value for term=record_place must not contain whitespace». **No working place filter was found on this endpoint.**

rows.lab: What this does, and does not, invalidate
rows.text:
**It does not invalidate the sweep's positive counts.** The method here already compensated: for each place the top hundred were pulled and **kept only if the record's own place text actually named that town**. That check is what makes the numbers above mean anything, and it is why they were published as *weight, not population*.

**It does sharpen the blanks.** Thirty-nine places returned nothing, and this page already said a blank proves nothing because those registers are browse-only and unindexed. There is now a **second** reason: the search can only ever see what ranks into the top hundred of a re-ranked list of 3,652 records. A blank is a statement about ranking, not about a province.

**And it retires a queue item.** This archive was carrying «Vižinada — 53 records, unread». Those records are on **DGS 005497893**, which is the **Vodnjan** baptism film, and they have now been read: they are the eight Vodnjan households. The item was a ghost of the two-parish reel.

rows.lab: The method that does work
rows.text:
**Resolve each record to the film it sits on, then ask the catalogue what that film is.** That is what produced this archive's ninety-three-parish list, and it is what found Vodnjan.

With one caution learned the same day: **a film can carry more than one parish**, and the catalogue answers a film-number query with the first creator on the reel. Resolve to the film, then read the item list — not the film heading. *(doc — every claim on this page was produced by running the queries and is reproducible)*

filter.source_filter: FamilySearch persona search endpoint, tested 9 September 2026 against ten place values including two nonsense controls.

surnames.heading: And the surname does not filter either — twenty-one towns that were never ours
surnames.lead: The place parameter was tested in September and found to be a relevance boost rather than a filter. This is the other half of the same lesson, and it was found by asking a much duller question: **which towns in our own register have no entry in our own atlas?** Twenty-one of them, holding forty-two rows between them. **Thirty-two of the forty-two carry a surname that is not a Franceschi form at all.**

rows.lab: What the thirty-two actually say
rows.text:
**Franceschini** at Krk — nine rows, 1676 to 1742, the largest single block. **Francetich** at Kastav — six, 1736 to 1861. **Defrančichi** at Pomer — three. **Franceschić** and **Franceschich** at Skitača — two, and they are the same woman twice. **Franceschin** at Lovran and Lovrana — two, and those are the same place twice. **Franciscolich** at Lussinpiccolo. **Francescon** at Knin. **Franchini** at Grobnik, at Pag and at Oprtalj.

These are not spellings of our name. They are other surnames — several of them formed from the same Latin root, in a province where that root is everywhere — and the index gathered them because the search was built to be generous. Generous is right for a first pass. It is wrong for a map.

rows.lab: Which makes Oprtalj a correction, not a target
rows.text:
On 13 September this archive drew up a round of fifteen Istrian towns to work, and put **Oprtalj** on it — sixteenth on the parish table, five indexed rows, a book filmed from 1815. The five rows are *Andreas Vesnaver Franecich*, *Catharina Franceschini*, *Catharina Francaschini*, *Anna Franchini* and *Joannes Vesnaver Franocich*.

**None of them is ours.** The target was made out of a count, and the count was made out of a fuzzy match. The plan was wrong within the hour of being written, which is the argument for checking a list against its own rows before working it.

rows.lab: Six rows survive, and one of them is a household
rows.text:
Of the forty-two, six carry a Franceschi form: two at **Sovinjak**, one at **Tar**, one at **Pag**, one at **Makarska**, one at **Nerežišća** on Brač.

Sovinjak is the one worth the walk. **Zuane Franceschi, buried there in 1759, son of Gio Batta Franceschi.** **Sebastiano De Franceschi, born and buried on 6 August 1783, son of Gio Battista De Franceschi.** One small hill parish above Buzet; two sons of a man of that name, twenty-four years apart. Either a father who buried a son in middle age and another in old age, or two generations keeping the grandfather's name — which is what this family does everywhere else it can be watched.

**It cannot be settled from a screen.** Sovinjak is not one of the parishes in the filmed collection this archive has walked, and neither is Šterna. *(Corrected the same day: Draguč, named here as equally unfilmed, is filmed — three volumes — and was tested image by image on 13 September. It holds none of the name.)*

surnames.source_sn: Computed from register.json against places.json on 13 September 2026, and checked row by row against the index's own surname field.

byimage.heading: Twenty parishes read by image instead of by place
byimage.lead:
Every sweep on this page until today matched records to towns by the **place text written in the index**. For Istria that text is very often «Croazia, Austria» and nothing more — no town at all — so every place-based count here has been built on the minority of records that happen to name one. The fix is to stop reading the place field. **Every image on FamilySearch is bound into a parish's book, and the book is the parish.** Fetch the image list under each of a parish's volumes, then match records to parishes by **image ark**. A record cannot be at the wrong parish if the page it is written on is in that parish's register.

Done that way against a pool of **1,768 distinct indexed records**, **forty-three Istrian parishes were tested. Twenty-two carry the name; twenty-one do not** — and six of the twenty-one had been counted here as carrying it.
table: The largest. Fifty-one spelt Defranceschi, thirty-three Defranceski, four with the háček.

Thirty-eight of the eighty-five are ours. The other forty-seven are Franceschini and Franceschina — a second, larger family at Pula that is not this one, and that every previous count here silently folded in.
Forty-two, and every one of them ours. See below: most of what this page has been calling the Pula cluster is Fažana.
Joined to Kaštelir and Tar below.
The 1569, 1583 and 1592 entries are Fracischetto, Francoscheto and Franceschero — not ours. Rovinj begins in 1619.
Six of the fourteen are Franceschich, Francescich, Francocich — Slavic formations, not ours.
And the 1684 is the find of the day. Below.
Three records and one whole household.
One, and undated. Bale's books run from 1538 and are effectively empty of the name.
Nine records, none of them ours: Franceschini ×5, Franchini, Francocich, Petrina.
One woman, one village, eleven entries — and she is on the lost-daughters queue.
Two De Franceschi women, two Domazetović men.

rows.lab: Pazin, 24 March 1684 — a century earlier than this archive had it
rows.text: «**Die 24 huius — Ego qui supra baptizavi Mariam filiam legitimam Francisci de Franceschi et uxoris eius Marinę. Patrini fuerunt Hilarius Celin[?] et Jacoba eiusdem…**» Pazin, *Births 1582, 1614–1624, 1645, 1643–1685*, read at full magnification. This archive's earliest Pazin record was **1791**. This is **1684** — a hundred and seven years earlier, and it is a household: a father, a wife, a legitimate daughter, two godparents. Why it matters more than its age. Kobler has a Giovanni Battista reaching Fiume **from the County of Pazin «intorno al 1740»**, and that departure has never been looked for at the departing end. A De Franceschi family is now documented in the county town **fifty-six years before the date Kobler gives**. That is not proof of a connection and is not offered as one. It is the first time the question can be asked of a real household instead of an assumption. Inferred **And the index has it wrong twice.** It transcribes the surname as «De Francesch», dropping the -i that the page plainly writes; and it puts **Jacoba — a godparent — into the mother's field**. The mother is **Marina**.

rows.lab: Vižinada, Kaštelir and Tar are one family, and now it can be drawn
rows.text: The lines chart has carried these three, with Šterna and Draguč, as «the Poreč hinterland» — *the largest piece of Istria the archive can document and cannot yet explain*. Three of the five now explain themselves, because the same people are in all three books. **Mattio**, whose son is buried at Vižinada in 1750. **Giulio (Julius) De Franceschi × Maria Ceselin — also written Sesalin and Cedelini** — whose son **Francesco Napoleone** is baptised at **Vižinada on 7 September 1818**, whose daughter Catharina is baptised at **Kaštelir in 1829**, and who is himself buried at **Kaštelir on 19 September 1854**, entered as «Giulio Defranceschi, of Mattio». **Francesco Napoleone** then appears at Kaštelir with a wife, **Maria Radojković**, and three children — Aloisia 1859, Josephus 1862, Margarita 1869. And the second household: **Angelus Defranceschi × Lucia-Antonia Rodella**, whose son **Julius is baptised at Kaštelir on 29 January 1866** — and buried at **Tar on 9 March 1870**, aged four. Angelus himself dies at Tar on 23 April 1895, aged sixty-seven. The Tar page on this site was written yesterday from the Tar entries alone, and could not say where the child was born. Kaštelir says. Inferred — the join is by name, date and parish adjacency, not by a document that names both places

rows.lab: Draguč does not exist, and five more blanks are now real blanks
rows.text:
The parish table on this page gives **Draguč 25 records, 1784–1851**. The September filter test had already shown that Vižinada and Draguč return *the same records in the same order*, and suspected the Draguč figure was Vižinada's set counted twice.

**It was.** Draguč's three volumes were fetched and every image ark in them tested against the pool: **zero**. The twenty-five were never there.

Five more come back empty on the same test, and these are now tested blanks rather than untested ones: **Kanfanar** (four books — and it adjoins Svetvinčenat, where the family is thickest), **Tinjan**, **Roč** (ten books from 1651), **Novigrad** (twenty books from 1662), **Marčana**.

rows.lab: Most of the «Pula» cluster is Fažana
rows.text:
The table at the head of this page names the Pula cluster's people as «**Natale Mattio, Angelo, Vitorio, Elisabetta, Irene De Franceschi**», 1778–1890.

Read by image, **Natale Mattio, Vittorio, Elisabetta and Irene are all in the Fažana register**, not Pula's — children of two households four miles up the coast. **Vittorio De Franceschi × Stella Tamborin** (written Etella, Steffa and Samburin in four different entries) baptise Perina in 1810, Vittorio in 1813 and **Natale Mattio on 21 April 1816**. **Giuseppe De Franceschi × Giovanna Beluzzi** baptise Elisabetta in 1810 and Irene on 13 October 1816.

Fažana has **forty-two records, all of them ours** — more than any Istrian parish except Ližnjan, Pula and Svetvinčenat, and it has been drawn on this site as a single dot reading «Baptisms and deaths at Fasana through the 1810s».

rows.lab: Two households that begin and end inside the record
rows.text: **Vrsar, 1670–1686.** «Luca De Franceschi, son of **Francesco De Franceschi and Giacoma**», baptised 11 August 1670. Giacoma buried 1683. A Marga «of Francesco» buried 19 August 1686. **Francesco himself buried 26 November 1686.** Five entries; a marriage, children, a widowing and a death, and then the name stops at Vrsar. **Rovinj, 1722–1728.** **Mattio De Franceschi × Elisabetta** baptise Martino in 1722 and Benedetto on 23 October 1726. **Isabetta is buried on 4 December 1728 and Matto on the 27th** — three weeks apart. And this archive already holds that 27 December entry from another direction: «**Ob.to di Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano**». So the man buried at Rovinj at Christmas 1728 and described from outside as *from Dignano* had been living there long enough to baptise two sons, and buried his wife three weeks before he died. Inferred — that the Isabetta of 4 December is the wife and not a daughter

rows.lab: And one of the twenty-six lost daughters, found at Krbune
rows.text:
The register page on this site carries a queue of **twenty-six De Franceschi women who married out and are attached to no household**, with forty indexed children hanging off them. Every one of those rows has **an empty place field** — that is precisely why they were never worked.

The image test places one of them. **Krbune** is a single-volume parish of 124 images in the County of Pazin, four kilometres from Gologorica. Its book holds **Mariana De Franceschi and her husband Vincentius Marziol** with five children between 1832 and 1843 — *Maria*, *Rosaria* 1833, *Franciscus* 21 November 1836, *Anna* 16 November 1839, *Antonia* 17 March 1843 — plus four more entries where the couple stand as godparents to other families' children.

She looked like several women because **the index spells her husband four ways** — *Marziol*, *Marizo*, *Marjas*, *Marjiol* — and her own name *Mariana*, *Marianna* and, in the Croatian orthography of the 1830s, **«Marianna Defrančeški»**. One woman, one village, eleven entries.

And the village matters: **Krbune is inside the County of Pazin**, the same small country as Gologorica and Gračišće, where this archive's own line lives.

rows.lab: Kršan: two De Franceschi women and two Domazetović men
rows.text: **Kršan** holds five records, all late and all of the same kind. **Anna Maria Francisca De Franceschi × Thomas Joachimus Clemens de Domazetovich** — children in 1881, 1883 and 1887. **Clotildis Adelaidis Defranceschi × Rudolfus Stanislaus de Domazetovich** — children in 1893 and 1894. Two women of the name marrying two men of one family, inside twelve years, in a parish where the surname appears nowhere else. Whether they are sisters the register does not say. The particle on *de Domazetovich* says the family they married into kept one. Inferred that the two women are of one household

byimage.source_bi: FamilySearch waypoint image lists for thirty Istrian parishes in Croatia, Church Books 1516-1994 (collection 2040054), intersected against 1,768 distinct indexed records gathered on 13 September 2026. The Pazin 1684 entry was read tile by tile from the Deep Zoom service at full magnification. Counts marked «ours» exclude Franceschini, Franceschina, Franceschich, Francocich, Fracischetto and the other formations of the same root that the index's fuzzy matching returns.

noplace.heading: Measuring the forty-five per cent, and a finer key than the film
noplace.lead: **Read the parish-map section at the foot of this page first — it got here before this did.** That section already says the Croatian index «usually gives no parish», and already resolves records through their image ark to a film number and the film to a parish. What follows **measures** that, extends the search that feeds it, and replaces the film-to-catalogue step with a finer one. It does not discover it. A correction to that effect is on the corrections page. The measurement: of **1,619 distinct indexed records** of the name in the Croatian church books, **727 — forty-five per cent — carry no town at all.** Their place field is empty, or it says «Croazia, Austria», «Hrvatska, Österreich», «Kraljevina Hrvatska». **They are not anonymous.** Every one carries the number of the microfilm it was photographed on.

rows.lab: Two more search keys, and the second is the one that matters
rows.text:
`q.fatherSurname` was found this morning. `q.motherSurname` works the same way, and it is the field **the married-out daughters live in** — a child with its father's surname, its mother entered as a De Franceschi. It returned **218 records the surname search had never seen**.

And every record carries `FS_DIGITAL_FILM_NBR` — the DGS film number — whether or not it carries a place. The place is optional. **The film never is.**

rows.lab: What the film alone gives back: 396 of the 727
rows.text:
Looked up one film at a time in the catalogue, **396 of the 727 town-less records resolve to a single parish**:

**Svetvinčenat 102 · Pula 83 · Dubrovnik-Grad 47 · Sv. Dujam, Split 46 · Rijeka 31 · Split-Veli Varoš 15 · Labin 10 · Nerežišća on Brač 10 · Dubrovnik-Pile 9 · Rovinj 7 · Barban 6 · Kastav 6 · Vižinada 5 · Split-Stari Grad 5 · Imotski-Glavina 4 · Split-Bol 4 · Vrsar 3 · Poreč 3.**

**Dubrovnik is the surprise.** Fifty-six town-less records between the city parish and Pile, against the twenty-two and sixteen the parish table has carried. And the Split parishes together hold about seventy. Neither city is on any lane of the branch chart.

rows.lab: And 331 sit on reels that carry more than one parish
rows.text:
The remaining **331** cannot be resolved by film number, because **one microfilm can carry two or more parishes' books**. This archive learned that in September and wrote it into the correction itself — *«remembering that a film can carry more than one parish»*. What is new here is only the size of it:

**005497884** carries **Svetvinčenat *and* Petar u Šumi**. **005497893** carries **Vižinada *and* an unnamed State Archive item**. **005494211** carries two Split parishes; **005494036** carries four; **005494037** carries seven.

So the film number is a fast first pass and not an answer — which the September note already said. The improvement is to stop relying on remembering: **resolve the ark to the book waypoint rather than to the film.** An image is bound into exactly one book and a book belongs to exactly one parish, so the ambiguity never arises instead of having to be caught.

rows.lab: The measurement that proves it — 110 records that would have been mislabelled
rows.text:
Film **005497893** carries **112** town-less records of the name. Its catalogue creator is «Rimokatolička crkva, **Župa Vižinada**».

Tested image by image against Vižinada's own books: **two of the hundred and twelve are Vižinada's.** The other hundred and ten are on the second item bound onto the same reel — the books this archive established in September are **Vodnjan's**.

Had these been assigned by the film's catalogue creator, as would have been the obvious thing to do, **110 records would have been filed under the wrong parish**, forty kilometres away. That is the same reel, and the same mistake, that produced «Vižinada, five households 1816–1844» — a finding this archive published and then had to withdraw as a ghost.

rows.lab: Šterna has a film after all
rows.text:
Yesterday's note said **Šterna** is not among the parishes in the filmed collection this archive has walked, and left it needing a different route.

It has one. **Film 005497888** carries five town-less records of the name, and its catalogue entry names two parishes: **Šterna** and **Šumber**. Which of the two holds them is the ark test, and the ark test is what stopped: after roughly two hundred catalogue and waypoint calls in a few minutes, FamilySearch returned **403**. That is a throttle, not a wall, and the work resumes on the other side of it.

The archive's own pacing note has said this since the Vodnjan tiles: *pace it*. Today it was ignored and the answer cost an hour.

noplace.source_np: Computed 13 September 2026 from 1,619 distinct persona records in FamilySearch collection 2040054, gathered by surname, father's surname and mother's surname; film numbers taken from each record's own FS_DIGITAL_FILM_NBR field and resolved through the FamilySearch catalogue; the 005497893 test run against the Vižinada waypoint image lists.
